doc.title: Robert Glasper interviewed by Greg Thomas, Clinton, New York, February 20, 2016

title: What a producer should do
summary: Glasper brings out the best in an artist rather than stamping his own sound; Quincy Jones and Michael Jackson's Off the Wall as example.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Which means that you have the ability to be able to — well let me let you explain. Now you mentioned yourself as a composer, as a player. As a producer, explain how you see your role as a producer.
I mean as a producer, as far as my own stuff or producing other people?
Well as a producer the thing a great producer is supposed to do is bring the best out of that person, what they are.
Yeah, exactly. Bring, you know, some producers, when they produce something you hear it and you’re like okay so-and-so produced that. I hear it.
Mmm. You could hear the stamp of the producer.

Hear the stamp of the producer. Which is not always bad. You know you hear something Babyface did, you’re like, “that’s Babyface.” You know? Duh. That’s Face. You know. You get it. That’s R. Kelly. You know? Certain producers have a thing, and some people want that thing. Because that thing sells and that’s what — you kind of want people to know that’s you, and that’s a different kind of producing. But from what I’m doing, I like to bring the best out of that particular artist, so I try to dwell in what they — where they live and figure that out and then go from there.

Yeah, Quincy does that. Exactly. Exactly. They didn’t want Quincy producing Michael [Jackson] because he was a jazz guy. They didn’t want him doing “Off the Wall.” Michael had to fight for Quincy to do “Off the Wall,” because he was the jazz guy. He never really did R&B like that you know. And boom.
